# <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

## <mark>Skin and Mucous Membrane Involvement</mark>

<mark>The characteristic skin lesion of bullous pemphigoid is a large, tense blister that arises on normal-appearing skin or on an erythematous base.</mark> These lesions most commonly occur on the lower abdomen, inner or anterior thighs, and flexor surfaces of the forearms, although they can appear anywhere on the body. <mark>The bullae are typically filled with clear fluid but may be hemorrhagic.</mark> <mark>After rupture, the erosions usually reepithelialize well and do not expand peripherally, unlike in pemphigus vulgaris.</mark> New vesicles may, however, develop at the edges of resolving lesions. <mark>Bullous pemphigoid lesions do not scar, and pruritus is commonly present, though not universally.</mark>

<mark>In some cases, the erythematous component predominates, and patients may initially present with urticarial plaques, particularly early in the disease course.</mark> The erythema can have a serpiginous pattern with peripheral blistering and may be extensive. Healing typically begins in the center of the lesions and may be accompanied by hyperpigmentation.

Mucous membrane involvement occurs in approximately 10% to 35% of patients and is almost always confined to the oral mucosa, particularly the buccal mucosa. Lesions may appear as intact blisters or, more commonly, as erosions. These do not scar and are usually not widespread. Notably, the vermilion border of the lips is rarely affected, distinguishing it from erythema multiforme.

## Unusual Clinical Presentations

Bullous pemphigoid can present in atypical forms, all confirmed by characteristic immunofluorescence findings. In some cases, the disease is localized, most frequently to the lower legs. Patients with localized disease have antibodies against the same pemphigoid antigens (BP180 and BP230) as those with generalized disease and may either remain localized for years or progress to generalized involvement.

A distinct variant occurs in young girls, characterized by blisters and erosions limited to the vulvar and perivulvar regions. As in other localized and childhood forms, autoantibodies target the classic pemphigoid antigens.

Early in the disease, some patients may exhibit only urticarial or eczematous lesions without frank bullae. Other rare presentations include erythroderma, prurigo nodularis-like lesions, vegetating lesions, and dyshidrotic dermatitis-like eruptions. <mark>Despite the atypical morphology, the immunopathological findings—such as linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone and reactivity with BPAG2 (BP180)—remain consistent with bullous pemphigoid.</mark>

## <mark>Non-autoimmune diseases</mark>

### <mark>Main differential diagnoses for DH: non-autoimmune diseases</mark>

Scabies  
<mark>Scabies may closely mimic the pruritic, vesicular, and papular lesions of dermatitis herpetiformis (DH), particularly in the early stages.</mark> <mark>The presence of burrows, preferential involvement of finger webs, wrists, elbows, and genitalia, and intense nocturnal itching are suggestive of scabies.</mark> <mark>A definitive diagnosis is achieved by identifying *Sarcoptes scabiei* mites, eggs, or fecal matter in skin scrapings examined under microscopy.</mark>

<mark>Irritant or allergic contact dermatitis</mark>  
<mark>These conditions can present with pruritic papules, vesicles, and erythematous plaques, resembling DH, especially when distributed on the elbows, knees, or buttocks.</mark> <mark>However, contact dermatitis typically correlates with exposure to specific allergens or irritants and lacks the symmetrical, chronic-relapsing pattern seen in DH.</mark> <mark>Patch testing can aid in identifying the responsible agent.</mark>

Atopic dermatitis  
<mark>Atopic dermatitis may present with pruritic, eczematous lesions that could be confused with the eczema-like variant of DH.</mark> <mark>However, atopic dermatitis usually affects flexural areas, has a personal or family history of atopy, and lacks the characteristic immunopathological findings of DH, such as granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae.</mark>

Arthropod bite reactions  
<mark>Reactions to insect bites can manifest as grouped or linearly arranged papules and vesicles (often referred to as "breakfast, lunch, and dinner" lesions), which may resemble the agminated vesicles of DH.</mark> <mark>A detailed history of outdoor exposure and the transient nature of bite reactions help differentiate them from the persistent, symmetrical lesions of DH.</mark>

Pityriasis lichenoides chronica  
<mark>This condition presents with recurrent crops of small, scaly, reddish-brown papules that may occasionally have a vesicular appearance.</mark> <mark>It typically affects the trunk and limbs and may be mistaken for the papulovesicular stage of DH.</mark> <mark>However, it lacks the intense pruritus and characteristic IgA deposition seen in DH.</mark>

Dyshidrotic eczema  
<mark>Also known as pompholyx, this condition is characterized by deep-seated vesicles on the palms, soles, and lateral aspects of the fingers—sites also commonly affected in DH.</mark> <mark>However, dyshidrotic eczema is not associated with gluten sensitivity and shows spongiosis and vesicle formation on histology without neutrophilic microabscesses or IgA deposits.</mark>

<mark>Drug eruptions</mark>  
<mark>Certain drug-induced eruptions (e.g., those caused by vancomycin, amphetamines, or anticonvulsants) can present with pruritic papulovesicular lesions resembling DH.</mark> <mark>A thorough medication history and resolution of lesions upon drug withdrawal support the diagnosis of a drug eruption.</mark> <mark>Additionally, these lack the specific immunopathological features of DH.</mark>

# <mark>Androgens</mark>

<mark>It has long been recognized that sebaceous glands require androgenic stimulation to produce significant quantities of sebum.</mark> <mark>Individuals with a genetic deficiency of androgen receptors (complete androgen insensitivity) have no detectable sebum secretion and do not develop acne.</mark> <mark>However, there is still a question as to which androgen is physiologically significant.</mark> <mark>Although the most powerful androgens are testosterone and its end-organ reduction product dihydrotestosterone, levels of testosterone do not parallel the patterns of sebaceous gland activity.</mark> <mark>For example, testosterone levels are many-fold higher in males than in females, with no overlap between the sexes, whereas average rates of sebum secretion are only slightly higher in males than in females, with considerable overlap between the groups.</mark> <mark>Also, sebum secretion starts to increase in children during adrenarche, a developmental event that precedes puberty by approximately 2 years.</mark>

<mark>The weak adrenal androgen dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) might be a significant regulator of sebaceous gland activity through its conversion to testosterone and dihydrotestosterone in the sebaceous gland.</mark> <mark>Levels of DHEAS are high in newborns, are very low in 2- to 4-year-old children, and start to rise when sebum secretion starts to increase.</mark> <mark>In adulthood, DHEAS levels show considerable individual variation but are only slightly higher in men than in women on the average.</mark> <mark>There is a decline in DHEAS levels in both sexes starting in early adulthood and continuing throughout life.</mark> <mark>This decline parallels the decline of sebum secretion.</mark> <mark>DHEAS is present in the blood in high concentration.</mark> <mark>The enzymes required to convert DHEAS to more potent androgens are present in sebaceous glands.</mark> <mark>These include $3\beta$-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, $17\beta$-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, and $5\alpha$-reductase.</mark> <mark>Each of these enzymes exists in two or more isoforms that exhibit tissue-specific differences in their expression.</mark> <mark>The predominant isozymes in the sebaceous gland include type 1 $3\beta$-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, type 2 $17\beta$-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, and type 1 $5\alpha$-reductase.</mark>

# Retinoids

Isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid) is the most potent pharmacologic inhibitor of sebum secretion. Significant reductions in sebum production can be observed as early as 2 weeks after use. Histologically, sebaceous glands are markedly reduced in size, and individual sebocytes appear undifferentiated, lacking the characteristic cytoplasmic accumulation of sebaceous lipids.

Isotretinoin does not interact with any of the known retinoid receptors. It may serve as a prodrug for the synthesis of all-trans retinoic acid or 9-cis retinoic acid, which do interact with retinoid receptors; however, it has greater sebosuppressive action than all-trans or 9-cis retinoic acid. The mechanism by which 13-cis retinoic acid lowers sebum secretion is unknown, but it inhibits the $3\alpha$-hydroxysteroid activity of retinol dehydrogenase and leads to decreased androgen synthesis. In addition, isotretinoin triggers cell cycle arrest in human sebocytes and immortalized cell culture models of human sebocytes (SZ95 and SEB-1) and also induces apoptosis in SEB-1 sebocytes. Inhibition of androgen synthesis, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis by 13-cis retinoic acid may explain the reduction of sebaceous gland size after treatment.

# Melanocortins

Melanocortins include melanocyte-stimulating hormone and adrenocorticotropic hormone. In rodents, melanocortins increase sebum production. Transgenic mice deficient in the melanocortin-5 receptor have hypoplastic sebaceous glands and reduced sebum production. The melanocortin-5 receptor has been identified in human sebaceous glands, where it may play a role in the modulation of sebum production.

# Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptors

PPARs are orphan nuclear receptors that are similar to retinoid receptors in many ways.

# Section 2. Highlights: Acne Pathogenesis and Role of Diet

## Key Points

- <mark>Acne originates in the **pilosebaceous unit**, primarily affecting areas with high density of these units such as the **face, neck, and upper torso**</mark>  
- <mark>**Inflammation** is a central driver in acne development, present from the earliest preclinical stages through to lesion formation and scarring</mark>  
- <mark>The **pathophysiology of acne is multifactorial**, involving:</mark>
  <mark>- Increased **sebum production**</mark>
  <mark>- **Hyperproliferation of keratinocytes** within the sebaceous follicle</mark>
  <mark>- **Follicular hyperkeratinization**</mark>
  <mark>- **Colonization by *Cutibacterium acnes*** (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*)</mark>
  <mark>- **Inflammatory responses**</mark>

## Acne Pathophysiology

Acne is a complex, multifactorial disorder centered on the pilosebaceous unit. <mark>$^{1,27,28}$ Advances in molecular research have revealed that inflammation is triggered when growth factors and androgens activate the pilosebaceous unit.</mark> <mark>Inflammation plays a critical role at every stage of acne—beginning with the formation of the **microcomedone**, the precursor to visible lesions, and extending to long-term consequences such as **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and scarring**.</mark> <mark>$^{29–32}$</mark>

<mark>This inflammatory process occurs concurrently with:</mark>
- <mark>Excess **sebum production**</mark>
- <mark>Abnormal **keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation**</mark>
- <mark>Colonization and amplification of inflammation by ***Cutibacterium acnes*** within the follicular duct, particularly in the infra-infundibulum (Fig. 3). $^{28}$</mark>

Figure 4 summarizes the proposed sequence of events in acne development, although the exact temporal order remains incompletely defined. <mark>$^{28}$ Current evidence suggests that **insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)** and **androgens** (e.g., DHEA-S) act synergistically—especially during puberty—to stimulate sebaceous gland activity.</mark> <mark>$^{28,33}$ These hormonal signals induce both increased sebum volume and qualitative changes in sebum composition, including:</mark>
- <mark>↓ Linoleic acid levels (due to sebaceous gland hyperplasia)</mark>
- <mark>↑ Squalene and lipid peroxides</mark>
- <mark>↑ Ratio of saturated to monounsaturated fatty acids $^{33–36}$</mark>

Multiple additional factors influence sebum regulation, including environmental exposures, neuroendocrine signals, and inflammatory mediators. Emerging data indicate that **endocannabinoids**, **ectopeptidases**, **corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH)**, **α-MSH**, **histamine**, **acetylcholine**, and others bind to receptors on sebocytes and may modulate their function in acne-prone skin. $^{37}$

Structural differences are also observed in acne-prone individuals:
- Greater number of **lobules per sebaceous gland**
- Larger **follicular diameter** $^{38}$
- Thicker, denser **follicular corneocyte lamellae**
- Reduced single-cell desquamation, promoting follicular occlusion $^{38}$

Additionally, sebocytes on the face exhibit a heightened response to androgens compared to those on non-acne-prone areas like the legs, which may explain the typical facial and truncal distribution of acne. $^{39}$

Androgens and growth factors also stimulate follicular keratinocytes, leading to:
- **Hyperproliferation**
- Altered differentiation
- Shift from individual cell shedding to cohesive clumping at the follicular orifice

Histologically, affected follicular walls show increased:
- Lipid vacuoles
- Filaggrin
- Tonofilaments

The pilosebaceous unit—particularly sebocytes—plays an active role in **skin endocrine function**. $^{40}$ Sebaceous glands secrete sebum via **holocrine secretion**, where mature sebocytes undergo programmed disintegration involving DNA degradation before releasing lipids into the sebaceous duct. This process is distinct from apoptosis or necroptosis. $^{41}$

Sebaceous gland activity is regulated by:
- **Androgen hormones**
- **Growth-promoting hormones**
- **Growth factors** (e.g., IGF-1)

## <mark>Pathogenesis of Acne</mark>

<mark>Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) is a weak androgen that is converted to the more potent testosterone by $3\beta$-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD) and $17\beta$-HSD.</mark> <mark>$5\alpha$-reductase then converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the predominant hormonal effector on the sebaceous gland.</mark> <mark>The sebaceous gland expresses each of these enzymes.</mark>  

**Key abbreviations**:  
- A = androstenedione  
- ACTH = adrenocorticotropic-stimulating hormone  
- DHEAS = dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate  
- E = estrogen  
- FSH = follicle-stimulating hormone  
- LH = luteinizing hormone  
- T = testosterone  

Subnormal levels of linoleic acid may induce follicular keratinocyte hyperproliferation and promote the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. It has also been suggested that normal quantities of linoleic acid are produced but become diluted due to increased sebum output.

Interleukin-1 (IL-1) may contribute to keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Human follicular keratinocytes exhibit hyperproliferation and microcomedone formation when exposed to IL-1. IL-1 receptor antagonists inhibit this process, supporting a role for IL-1 in acne pathogenesis.

### Excess Sebum Production

<mark>The second key feature in acne pathogenesis is excess sebum production by the sebaceous gland.</mark> <mark>Patients with acne produce more sebum than those without, although the qualitative composition remains similar.</mark> <mark>Triglycerides, a component of sebum, are broken down by *Cutibacterium acnes* (*P.</mark> <mark>acnes*), a normal resident of the pilosebaceous unit.</mark> <mark>This breakdown releases free fatty acids, which:</mark>

- <mark>Promote bacterial clumping and colonization of *P. acnes*</mark>  
- <mark>Induce inflammation</mark>  
- <mark>May have comedogenic properties</mark>  

<mark>Androgenic hormones significantly influence sebum production.</mark> <mark>Similar to their effects on follicular keratinocytes, androgens bind to receptors and modulate sebocyte activity.</mark> <mark>Individuals with acne tend to have higher average serum androgen levels than unaffected individuals, though these levels remain within the normal range.</mark> <mark>The enzyme $5\alpha$-reductase, responsible for converting testosterone to the more potent DHT, exhibits highest activity in acne-prone areas such as the face, chest, and back.</mark>

<mark>The role of estrogen in sebum production is less clear.</mark> <mark>The dose of estrogen required to reduce sebum production exceeds the dose needed to suppress ovulation.</mark> <mark>Proposed mechanisms by which estrogens may reduce sebum include:</mark>

1. <mark>Direct opposition of androgen effects within the sebaceous gland</mark>  
2. <mark>Inhibition of gonadal androgen production via negative feedback on pituitary gonadotropin (FSH/LH) release</mark>  
3. <mark>Regulation of genes that suppress sebaceous gland growth or lipid synthesis</mark>  

### <mark>Microcomedo Formation and Inflammation</mark>

The microcomedo expands due to accumulation of densely packed keratin, sebum, and bacteria. Progressive distension leads to follicular wall rupture. The extrusion of keratin, sebum, and microbial contents into the dermis triggers a robust inflammatory response.

Cellular infiltration follows a temporal pattern:
- Within 24 hours of rupture: **Lymphocytes** predominate  
  - $\mathrm{CD4^{+}}$ T cells localize around the pilosebaceous unit  
  - $\mathrm{CD8^{+}}$ T cells are found in perivascular regions  
- 1–2 days after rupture: **Neutrophils** become the dominant cell type surrounding the ruptured microcomedo  

Traditionally, inflammation was thought to follow comedo formation. However, emerging evidence suggests that dermal inflammation may precede microcomedo development. Biopsies of acne-prone, comedo-free skin show increased inflammatory markers compared to normal skin. Newly formed comedos exhibit even greater inflammation, indicating that immune activation may be an early event in acne pathogenesis. Further research is needed to clarify the sequence of these events.

### Role of *Cutibacterium acnes* in Inflammation

*Cutibacterium acnes* (*P. acnes*) plays an active role in inflammation. The fourth key element in acne pathogenesis, *P. acnes* contributes to immune activation through multiple mechanisms, including:
- Activation of toll-like receptors (TLRs), particularly TLR2 and TLR4  
- Induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1α, IL-8, TNF-α)  
- Promotion of inflammasome activation, leading to IL-1β release  

These actions amplify local inflammation and contribute to both comedogenesis and lesion progression.

# Etiology and Pathogenesis

<mark>Like estrogen receptors, androgen receptors are present throughout the skin.</mark> <mark>In men, androgens are synthesized in the testes and adrenals, whereas in women, androgens are secreted by the ovaries and adrenals.</mark> <mark>In addition to testosterone, progesterone, dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), and DHEA sulfate (DHEA-S) are natural androgens that can lead to cutaneous manifestations when present in excess.</mark> <mark>Testosterone is converted in peripheral tissues into the more potent androgen 5α-dihydrotestosterone (5α-DHT) by the enzyme 5α-reductase.</mark> <mark>Unlike testosterone, 5α-DHT cannot be aromatized to estrogen and therefore exerts purely androgenic effects.</mark> <mark>Furthermore, 5α-DHT binds to the androgen receptor with greater affinity than testosterone.</mark>

<mark>Androgens play a key role in regulating hair growth and sebaceous gland activity.</mark> <mark>They are also involved in wound healing, epidermal differentiation, and modulation of dermal fibroblasts.</mark> <mark>The distribution of androgen receptors correlates with the development of "male-pattern" hair growth on the face, chest, and back, as well as androgenetic alopecia on the scalp.</mark> Both estrogens and androgens can bind to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), also known as testosterone-estrogen-binding globulin (TEBG). SHBG levels are reduced by synthetic progestins found in oral contraceptives (e.g., norgestrel, norethindrone, norgestimate, desogestrel), as well as in conditions such as obesity, acromegaly, hypothyroidism, and hyperinsulinemia. Lower SHBG levels increase free circulating androgens, contributing to the development of androgenic symptoms in these states.

# Clinical Findings and Diagnosis: Cutaneous Manifestations of Androgen Excess

Androgen-related skin disorders are common in dermatology. <mark>Although the exact pathogenesis of acne remains incompletely understood, androgen stimulation of sebaceous glands is a well-established contributing factor.</mark> <mark>Acne typically improves after adolescence in most individuals (see Chap.</mark> 78). <mark>Persistent or late-onset acne should prompt consideration of underlying androgen excess, including conditions such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) in women, or an androgen-secreting tumor.</mark> Rosacea and chemically induced acne should also be included in the differential diagnosis. In appropriate clinical contexts, laboratory testing can help identify the source of androgen excess (see Table 152-13). Acne is also a common manifestation of androgen excess in individuals using performance-enhancing anabolic steroids, which are testosterone derivatives.

Genetic differences influence hair follicle sensitivity to androgens, explaining the variable expression of hirsutism among women exposed to similar androgen levels.

# Table 152-13 Approach to the Female Patient with Suspected Hyperandrogenism

**History and physical findings suggestive of hyperandrogenism**
- Sudden onset of acne  
- Severe acne unresponsive to standard therapy  
- Irregular menstrual cycles  
- Hirsutism  

**Laboratory evaluation** (most reliable when patient is off oral contraceptives for 4–6 weeks and testing is performed before menses)
- **Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S):** screens for adrenal source  
  - >8000 ng/mL: suggestive of adrenal tumor  
  - 4000–8000 ng/mL: consistent with congenital adrenal hyperplasia  
- **Testosterone:** screens for ovarian source  
  - 150–200 ng/dL: commonly seen in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)  
  - May also be elevated in some adrenal tumors  
- **Luteinizing hormone (LH) to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) ratio**  
  - >2–3: supports diagnosis of PCOS

Staphylococcal bacteremia may complicate either primary or secondary cutaneous infections such as psoriasis or scabies. - <mark>Treatment of the acute infection</mark>
- Management of underlying dermatoses
- Eradication of nasal *S. aureus* carriage using mupirocin (pseudomonic acid) ointment
- Long-term oral prophylaxis for recurrent infections

---

*Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (see Chap. 180) can cause primary cutaneous infections such as cellulitis (e.g., ecthyma gangrenosum), catheter-site infections, and secondary infections of underlying skin conditions like Kaposi sarcoma in advanced HIV disease.

Cutaneous *P. aeruginosa* infection occurs via:
- Local invasion through skin breaches
- Primary infection of skin appendages in the anogenital or axillary regions
- Hematogenous dissemination to the skin

These infections may progress to bacteremia, leading to seeding of multiple organ systems.

---

Tuberculosis is the most common opportunistic infection in HIV-infected individuals in developing countries. While cutaneous tuberculosis (see Chap. 184) is relatively uncommon, the incidence of extrapulmonary tuberculosis is higher in HIV-positive individuals:
- 15% in non-HIV-infected individuals
- 20% to 40% in those with HIV disease
- Up to 70% in advanced HIV disease

- *M. chelonae*
- *M. fortuitum*
- *M. kansasii*
- *M. malmoense*
- *M. gordonae*
- *M. marinum*
- *M. haemophilum*

The most common non-tuberculous mycobacterial pathogen in advanced HIV disease is the *M. avium-intracellulare* complex (MAC). However, MAC rarely presents with cutaneous manifestations.
